readings.title: The Downy Woodpecker — the drummer (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a long paragraph that mixes careful watching with jokes, and tell which is which.
readings.focus: A bird with no song makes music by drumming, and Comstock watches pairs and rivals for years.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The downy is a small black-and-white woodpecker; the male has a red patch on the back of his head. James Whitcomb Riley was a popular American poet. A resonant branch rings or echoes when struck. A minx is a bold, saucy girl; suitors are males courting a mate; animosity is hatred; circumspect means careful. Suet is hard beef fat put out for birds in winter.
readings.contentNote: Comstock jokes about woodpecker husbands and wives in the language of her time (a “bold minx,” the “lord and master”); these are her jokes, not facts about birds or people.

excerpt.locator: “The Downy Woodpecker,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraph on drumming; opens “James Whitcomb Riley describes the drumming of the woodpecker as “weeding out the…”; closes “…and master is somewhat bossy, yet they seem to get along as well as most married pairs.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the woodpecker drum instead of sing? What does the male choose to drum on?
facilitatorNotes: He “has no voice for singing,” so when he is “musically inclined, he turns drummer.” He picks a dry limb of hard wood that rings well and comes back to it day after day.
evidence: The woodpecker has no voice for singing,
he turns drummer.

questions.prompt: What happened when Comstock saw a female drumming?
facilitatorNotes: She jokingly scolded her, but within twenty minutes two male suitors arrived and chased each other. So drumming by a female was “evidently not considered improper in woodpecker society.” The joke is on Comstock.
evidence: I once observed a female drumming.
she had drummed up two red-capped suitors

questions.prompt: How did two rival males fight? Why does Comstock call it “much fuss and no bloodshed”?
facilitatorNotes: They glared and bobbed their heads, but when they came close enough to stab each other, both backed away. It was all show.
evidence: much fuss and no bloodshed.
they beat a mutual and circumspect retreat.

questions.prompt: Comstock doubts that spring drumming is a call for a new wife. What does she think instead, and what evidence does she give?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks the male is telling his mate it is time to build a nest, because the pairs she watched for years came to the suet together all winter. Ask whether her evidence proves it or only makes it likely; she says “I believe,” not “I know.”
evidence: I believe they are, instead, calling the attention of their lawful spouses to the fact that it is time for nest building to begin.
have always come in pairs to partake of suet during the entire winter;

readings.title: The Flicker — a meadow-lark with a red mark (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Keep track of many colors and body parts, and decide which ones matter most for telling one bird from another.
readings.focus: A careful description that begins with a mistake and a single telling mark.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The flicker is a large woodpecker that often feeds on the ground. The nape is the back of the neck; the rump is the lower back, just above the tail.

excerpt.locator: “The Flicker or Yellow-hammer,” Teacher’s Story, first paragraph; opens “The first time I ever saw a flicker I said, “What a wonderful meadow-lark and what is it…”; closes “…nor does it stay so constantly in the meadows but often frequents woods and orchards.”.

questions.prompt: Which bird did the flicker remind Comstock of at first glance, and what single mark told her she was wrong?
facilitatorNotes: A meadow-lark; then she saw a red spot on the back of its neck, and once she was sure it was not a wound, she knew it was no meadow-lark.
evidence: What a wonderful meadow-lark
a red spot on the back of the bird’s neck,

questions.prompt: How can you tell a male flicker from a female?
facilitatorNotes: The male has a black mustache from the beak backward; the female looks like him but has none. Comstock jokes that the droop is “very fashionable.”
evidence: the male has a black mustache extending backward from the beak with a very fashionable droop.

questions.prompt: Why is the white patch on the flicker’s rump called a “color call”?
facilitatorNotes: It is a signal at the rear that helps a migrating flock keep together at night. It hardly shows when the bird sits still, so it works mainly in flight.
evidence: it being a rear signal by means of which the flock of migrating birds are able to keep together in the night.

questions.prompt: Choose three of the flicker’s marks. Which one would help you most to recognize a flicker in a meadow, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Any well-supported choice works: the red band on the nape, the black crescent “locket,” the spotted breast, the yellow under the wings in flight, or the wave-like, jerky flight. Ask which marks show only when the bird flies.
evidence: a bright red band across the nape of the neck.
There is a locket adorning the breast which is a thin, black crescent,

readings.title: The Catbird — a performer of many acts (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Separate what Comstock heard and saw from what she imagines the birds were feeling.
readings.focus: A noisy, clever mimic described as if it were a stage performer.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Vaudeville was a popular stage show of many short acts: singers, comedians, acrobats and impersonators, often in costume. A rod is about sixteen feet; a medley is a mixture of tunes; a mocker is a bird that copies other birds’ songs.

excerpt.locator: “The Catbird,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraph after the opening verse; opens “As a performer, the catbird distinctly belongs to the vaudeville, even going so far as to…”; closes “…his tail, like a brown thrasher; and again, he sings completely hidden in the thicket.”.

questions.prompt: How did the young catbirds behave when Comstock walked into their territory?
facilitatorNotes: They squalled loudly and followed her as she backed away, looking triumphant. She says they “obviously enjoyed” her fright: that is her reading of their behavior.
evidence: the squalling that ensued was ear-splitting;
they obviously enjoyed my apparent fright.

questions.prompt: What happened on the spring morning when Comstock heard a cardinal? What did she decide it meant?
facilitatorNotes: She rushed to the window and found a catbird singing the cardinal’s song. Cardinals were rare in New York, so she decided this catbird had spent the winter in the South among cardinals and learned their song there.
evidence: only to see a catbird singing the cardinal song,

questions.prompt: Comstock and Mr. Mathews disagree about the catbird’s true song. What does each of them think?
facilitatorNotes: Mathews thinks it is a medley of other birds’ songs; Comstock finds it “very individual,” its own. She still agrees the catbird is a true mocker, so both can be partly right.
evidence: Mr. Mathews thinks it is a medley gathered from other birds, but it seems to me very individual.

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock say the catbird belongs to vaudeville? Which details support the joke?
facilitatorNotes: Like a vaudeville performer it has many acts: lovely songs, scolding, a cat-like call slipped into its song, and imitations of robins and even chickens. Its plain gray feathers are its “slate-colored tights,” a costume.
evidence: As a performer, the catbird distinctly belongs to the vaudeville,
even going so far as to appear in slate-colored tights.

readings.title: The Screech Owl — a chilling song and a turning head (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Connect each of the owl’s features to the way it lives.
readings.focus: A night hunter whose song frightens people and whose eyes and neck are built for the dark.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The screech owl is a small owl of North American woods. An owlet is a young or small owl. Tremulous means trembling; quavers are trembling notes. The iris is the colored ring in the eye and the pupil the dark center; a pivot is a point something turns on.

excerpt.locator: “The Screech Owl,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on the song and the eyes; opens “Of all the fascinating sounds to be heard at night in the woods, the screech owl’s song…”; closes “…cat, has eyes fitted for night hunting, it can also see fairly well during the daytime.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the screech owl’s song so “fascinating,” according to Comstock? How does the owl himself hear it?
facilitatorNotes: Not because it is musical, but because it sends chills up and down the listener’s spine. To the owl it is “the most beautiful music in the world,” a call to his mate.
evidence: upon the chills which it sends up and down the spine of the listener,
the most beautiful music in the world;

questions.prompt: How are the owl’s eyes suited to hunting at night?
facilitatorNotes: They are very large, and the pupil opens until it covers most of the eye in the dark, like a cat’s.
evidence: The eyes are very large
in the night this pupil is expanded until it covers most of the eye.

questions.prompt: Why are the owl’s eyes in the front of its head, like ours? How does it see behind?
facilitatorNotes: It hunts rather than being hunted, so it needs to focus ahead on its prey. To look behind, it turns its head “as if it were fitted on a ball-bearing joint.”
evidence: The owl is a bird that hunts instead of being hunted,
the head turns upon the neck as if it were fitted on a ball-bearing joint.

questions.prompt: Describe Comstock’s experiment with the captive owl. What did she discover, and what did she not quite see?
facilitatorNotes: She walked around it; it followed her with its head almost all the way round, then snapped back so fast she could hardly see the movement. She had to guess how it turned. Ask why a watcher should say when something happened too fast to see.
evidence: I have often amused myself by walking around a captive screech owl,
the head would twist back with such lightning rapidity that I could hardly detect the movement;

readings.title: The Crow — both sides of the case (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a writer who weighs good and bad and admits her own likes and dislikes.
readings.focus: Whether an animal is “good” or “bad” depends on who is judging.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Suet is hard fat that people hang out in winter to feed small birds such as chickadees and nuthatches; nestlings are baby birds still in the nest.
readings.contentNote: Comstock hired a boy with a shotgun to kill crows that raided other birds’ nests, as people commonly did in her time.

excerpt.locator: “The Crow,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraph after Thoreau’s description; opens “The crow is probably the most intelligent of all our native birds. It is quick to learn…”; closes “…friend of several tame crows who were even more interesting than they were mischievous.”.

questions.prompt: What did crows learn about the devices farmers used to keep them out of the corn?
facilitatorNotes: That the devices were harmless, so they could ignore them. Comstock uses this as evidence of how intelligent crows are.
evidence: the harmless character of which the crow soon understood perfectly.

questions.prompt: Which crows does Comstock dislike, and which does she admire?
facilitatorNotes: She dislikes the old crow that steals her suet and the crows that raid robins’ nests; she admires a flock that worked in a nearby field and several tame crows she befriended.
evidence: I do not like at all the cunning old crow which steals the suet
I became a sincere admirer of a crow flock

questions.prompt: What does Comstock mean when she says the crow’s “virtues and … sins” are judged “from our standpoint”?
facilitatorNotes: A crow is called good or bad by what it does to people, their crops and the birds they like; the crow itself is simply living. That is why she asks readers to “listen to both sides” before judging.
evidence: as judged from our standpoint;
we should listen to both sides of the case before we pass judgment.

questions.prompt: “I find with crows, as with people, I like some more than I do others.” Is that a fair way to judge animals? Was her answer to the nest-raiding crows fair?
facilitatorNotes: She judges crows one by one instead of all alike. Some readers will think protecting the nestlings was right; others will say the crows were only doing what crows do. Ask for reasons from the paragraph.
evidence: I find with crows, as with people, I like some more than I do others.

readings.title: The Goldfish — a Midas touch made by people (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Connect an old story to a scientific explanation of how goldfish got their colors.
readings.focus: People made the goldfish golden by choosing which fish to breed, and wild goldfish turn green again.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. In the Greek story, King Midas was granted the wish that everything he touched would turn to gold. Goldfish first came from China (the “Orient” in old books). Selecting and breeding means choosing which animals will have young. Effulgent means shining; progeny are offspring; oxydized (oxidized) silver is darkened silver. The Delaware and Potomac are rivers in the eastern United States.

excerpt.locator: “The Goldfish,” Teacher’s Story, the first two paragraphs; opens “ONCE upon a time, if stories are true, there lived a king called Midas, whose touch…”; closes “…old in a school aquarium; and there is on record one goldfish that lived nine years.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock think of King Midas when she sees goldfish?
facilitatorNotes: They look as if someone with a golden touch had handled them. She jokes that Midas might have touched little fish in Chinese streams.
evidence: whose touch turned everything to gold.
I wonder if, perhaps, King Midas were not a Chinese

questions.prompt: What “magic” really made goldfish golden?
facilitatorNotes: People, by “selecting and breeding” the fish over a long time. Their wild ancestors in China were plain green.
evidence: it is through his agency in selecting and breeding that we have gained these exquisite fish
wore safe green colors like the shiners in our brooks;

questions.prompt: What happens to goldfish that escape into rivers? Why would a bright gold fish have trouble in the wild?
facilitatorNotes: Their young return to olive-green. A brilliant fish would be easy for bigger fish to see and eat, like “glittering bait”; green keeps a fish safe.
evidence: their progeny return to their native olive-green color.
should escape the fate of being eaten by some larger fish attracted by such glittering bait.

questions.prompt: What advice does Comstock give for keeping goldfish? Which piece surprises you most?
facilitatorNotes: Change the water at least twice a week, and do not overfeed: goldfish “are more likely to die from overfeeding than from starving.” They can live seven or nine years. Many readers are surprised that too much food is the danger.
evidence: these fish are more likely to die from overfeeding than from starving.
there is on record one goldfish that lived nine years.

readings.title: The Stickleback — a father who builds and guards (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a building process in order, then notice where the writer judges the fish as if they were people.
readings.focus: A small fish’s nest, and a father who stays to guard the eggs.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The stickleback is a small fish with sharp spines on its back. Algae (spelled “algæ” here) are tiny water plants; pectoral fins grow just behind the gills; milt is the fluid a male fish spreads over eggs so they can grow; wooing is courting. A polygamist is a husband with several wives, a joke here because the father invites several females to the nest.

excerpt.locator: “The Stickleback,” Teacher’s Story, the two paragraphs from “But it is as a house builder” through the hatching of the young; opens “But it is as a house builder and father and home protector that the stickleback shines.…”; closes “…mouths to the pond weeds until they become strong enough to scurry around in the water.”.

questions.prompt: What does the stickleback build his nest from, and what holds it together?
facilitatorNotes: Fine green algae called frog-spittle, fastened to grass stems with a waterproof glue that his own body makes and spins out in threads.
evidence: the fine green algæ called frog-spittle.
The glue is waterproof.

questions.prompt: Comstock says “home is his sphere literally.” What shape and size is the nest?
facilitatorNotes: A hollow ball about the size of a glass marble, three-quarters of an inch across, with a round door at the side. “Sphere” also means the place where someone belongs, so the sentence is a pun.
evidence: he builds a spherical house about the size of a glass marble,
he finishes his pretty structure with a circular door at the side.

questions.prompt: Once the eggs are in the nest, what jobs does the father do?
facilitatorNotes: He stands at the door fanning water over the eggs with his fins, attacks every intruder, and guards until the young hatch and float away.
evidence: sets up a current of water over the eggs;
he drives off all intruders with the most vicious attacks,

questions.prompt: Comstock calls the mother “a flighty creature.” Is she describing the fish, or judging them as if they were people? How might you say the same thing without judging?
facilitatorNotes: She is judging in a joking, human way. Plainly put: in this species the male cares for the eggs and the females leave after laying. Some readers will enjoy the jokes; others will notice they make the mother sound careless.
evidence: being a flighty creature, she sheds responsibilities and flits off care free.

readings.title: The Sunfish — a fish with more courage than wisdom (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Find out why one fish has so many names, and judge Comstock’s fishing story.
readings.focus: A small, bright, fierce fish described by its shape and its fighting spirit.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The sunfish, or pumpkinseed, is a small, round, brightly colored fish of North American ponds and streams. The dorsal fin is the fin on its back. Indomitable means impossible to defeat; eddies are swirls of water; “gamey” means full of fight on a fishing line; canny means clever.
readings.contentNote: Comstock compares the fin to “the head-dress of an Indian chief,” a common picture in her time that lumps many different Native nations together.

excerpt.locator: “The Sunfish,” Teacher’s Story, the first three paragraphs; opens “THIS little disc of gay color has won many popular names. It is called pumpkin seed,…”; closes “…and thus placed they are able to discern the enemy or the dinner coming from any quarter.”.

questions.prompt: List the sunfish’s names. Which ones come from its shape?
facilitatorNotes: Pumpkin seed, tobacco box and sunfish come from its shape; it is also called bream and pondfish. Comstock says “pumpkin seed” is the most graphic, because seen from the side it looks like one.
evidence: It is called pumpkin seed, tobacco box and sunfish because of its shape,
“pumpkin seed” is the most graphic,

questions.prompt: What happened when Comstock caught a sunfish? Why does she say it had “more courage than wisdom”?
facilitatorNotes: She thought it was a bass, threw it back, and within five minutes it grabbed her hook again. Brave, but not wise.
evidence: he grabbed my hook again within five minutes,
which showed that he had more courage than wisdom;

questions.prompt: Why didn’t Comstock keep the fish to eat?
facilitatorNotes: She “never could make up my mind to kill a fish for the sake of one mouthful of food.” It was too small to be worth a life to her.
evidence: I never could make up my mind to kill a fish for the sake of one mouthful of food.

questions.prompt: Seen from above, the sunfish is “widest at the eyes.” Why does Comstock call that “a canny arrangement”? What other shape does she compare it to?
facilitatorNotes: Its large eyes can turn in every direction to spot an enemy or a dinner. She compares the body to “a powerful craft,” a boat with a rounded nose. Readers may choose their own comparison.
evidence: it is widest at the eyes and this is a canny arrangement,
it has the shape of a powerful craft

readings.title: The Cotton-tail Rabbit — tracks in the snow (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Turn a written description into a picture, and read an animal’s signals.
readings.focus: Snow tracks and ear positions reveal a rabbit’s secret night life and its state of mind.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. “Molly Cotton-tail” is an old nickname for a mother rabbit. A vaulting pole is the long pole a jumper uses to spring over a bar; placidity means calm; a rabbit’s form is the shallow hollow where it rests.

excerpt.locator: “The Cotton-tail Rabbit,” Teacher’s Story, first two paragraphs; opens “IT is well for Molly Cotton-tail and her family that they have learned to shun more than…”; closes “…cotton-tail stands up on its haunches with both ears erect, it looks very tall indeed.”.

questions.prompt: How did Comstock know rabbits were wandering around her house at night?
facilitatorNotes: After each fresh snowfall she could follow their tracks around the house, under the spruces and through the orchard.
evidence: after each fresh fall of snow this winter we have been able to trace our bunny neighbors

questions.prompt: Describe a cotton-tail’s track. Why do the big hind prints land ahead of the small front ones?
facilitatorNotes: Two long prints side by side, with two smaller ones between and a little behind. The rabbit plants its front feet like a vaulting pole and swings its hind feet past them. The prints are blurry because its feet are hairy. Try drawing it.
evidence: the rabbit uses its front feet as a boy uses a vaulting pole
owing to the fact that the bottoms of the feet are hairy the print is not clear-cut.

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock say Molly “was very considerate” in the garden? Is she serious?
facilitatorNotes: The rabbit ate the grass in the cress bed and left the cress. Comstock is joking: the rabbit was eating what it liked, and she pretends it was being polite.
evidence: She carefully pulled all the grass out of the garden-cress bed, leaving the salad for our enjoyment.

questions.prompt: “The long, strong hind legs and the long ears tell the whole bunny story.” What story do they tell? What do the ears say?
facilitatorNotes: Ears hear the enemy and legs carry the rabbit away. Ears laid back mean calm but watchful; straight up, alert and anxious; one forward and one back, “where did that sound come from?”
evidence: Ears to hear the approach of the enemy, and legs to propel the listener by long jumps to a safe retreat.
Now just where did that sound come from?

readings.title: The Red Squirrel — observations and roads (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Find the place where Comstock says a squirrel is only pretending, and check her reason.
readings.focus: A squirrel’s comic poses, and the regular roads it keeps through the treetops.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Haunches are hips and back legs; affectation is pretending to feel something; warily means carefully, watching for danger. James Whitcomb Riley was a popular American poet of the time.

excerpt.locator: “The Red Squirrel or Chickaree,” Teacher’s Story, the two paragraphs after Thoreau’s description; opens “It is surely one of the most comical of sights to see a squirrel stop running and take…”; closes “…with the body, as if its wide brush helped to buoy him up and perhaps to steer him also.”.

questions.prompt: What does a squirrel do when it stops to “take observations”?
facilitatorNotes: It sits up on its haunches, bends forward and presses its paws against its chest, as if saying “Be still, oh my beating heart!”
evidence: he lifts himself on his haunches,
Be still, oh my beating heart!

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock call that gesture “pure affectation”?
facilitatorNotes: Because the squirrel is not really frightened: it knows it can get away safely. Some readers may wonder how Comstock can know what the squirrel knows.
evidence: which is all pure affectation because he knows he can scurry away in perfect safety.

questions.prompt: How does a squirrel hiding behind a tree give itself away?
facilitatorNotes: It peeps out and whisks back, but its tail sticks out: as Riley says, “he lets his own tail tell on him.”
evidence: he lets his own tail tell on him.

questions.prompt: What did Comstock find by keeping notes on squirrel paths near her home? Why might a squirrel be careful off its roads but reckless on them?
facilitatorNotes: Squirrels use the same roads, some with “air bridges” between particular branches. Off them they go warily; on them they rush. They know every jump on a familiar road but not on new ground.
evidence: Such a path may be entirely in the treetops, with air bridges
if a squirrel leaves them for exploring, he goes warily; while, when following them, he is quite reckless in his haste.

readings.title: The Little Brown Bat — mothers, twins and senseless fears (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Sort true facts from the false beliefs Comstock sets out to correct.
readings.focus: A gentle, useful animal that people fear for no good reason.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Bats are mammals: they have fur and feed their babies milk. To hibernate is to sleep through the winter. Unencumbered means without a load; tresses are long hair; a slander is a false story that harms someone’s name. Vampire bats, which live in Central and South America, feed on blood. Malaria is a disease carried by some mosquitoes.

excerpt.locator: “The Little Brown Bat,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on the young and on fears about bats; opens “The mother bat feeds her little ones from her breasts as a mouse does its young, only she…”; closes “…of an anatomical standpoint, we shall know what these leafy appendages are used for.”.

questions.prompt: How does a mother bat care for her babies?
facilitatorNotes: She feeds them milk while cradling them in her wings, takes them on her evening hunts clinging to her neck, and hangs them on a twig when she needs to work alone.
evidence: she cradles them in her soft wings while so doing;
she hangs her tiny youngsters on some twig and goes back to them later.

questions.prompt: What do bats do in winter, and when do they come out again?
facilitatorNotes: They hibernate in hollow trees or caves and wake when insects are flying again.
evidence: During the winter, bats hibernate like woodchucks or chipmunks.
do not awake until the insects are flying;

questions.prompt: Name two “senseless fears” about bats. How does Comstock answer each one?
facilitatorNotes: That a bat wants to tangle itself in a woman’s hair (it would frighten the bat more than the lady); that bats bring bedbugs (an “ungrateful slander,” since they come in for mosquitoes); that all bats are vampires (there are none in the United States).
evidence: a situation which would frighten him far more than the lady;
but there are no vampires in the United States.

questions.prompt: Comstock says scientists should study bats “from a nature-study instead of an anatomical standpoint.” What does she mean? Why might watching a live bat teach something that a dead one cannot?
facilitatorNotes: Anatomy studies a body’s parts, often from dead specimens; nature study watches what living animals do. To learn what the leaf-like growths on some bats’ noses are for, you would have to see them in use. (Scientists now know such bats use them in finding their way by sound.)
evidence: when scientists study the bat from a nature-study instead of an anatomical standpoint,
we shall know what these leafy appendages are used for.

readings.title: Dogs — how a dog shows what it feels (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Match each of a dog’s feelings with the signs that show it.
readings.focus: A dog speaks with its tail, ears and voice, and its howl comes from its wolf ancestors.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Ecstatic means wildly happy; beseechingly means begging. Dogs are descended from wolves, which hunt in groups called packs. Baying is the deep, long bark of a hound; a reversion is a return to an older habit; ancestral means coming from ancestors; shackles and trammels are chains and restraints.

excerpt.locator: “Dogs,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on a dog’s feelings and on barking and howling; opens “Of all domestic animals, the dog is most humanly understandable in expressing emotions.…”; closes “…for the time, enables us to free ourselves from all conventional shackles and trammels.”.

questions.prompt: Choose three feelings Comstock describes. How does a dog show each one?
facilitatorNotes: Delight: leaping, little barks, tail up. Friendliness: sniffing, then wagging. Anger: growling, teeth showing, tail stiff behind. Fear: whining and lying flat. Shame: tail between the legs, slinking away. Readers may add signs from dogs they know.
evidence: If delighted, he leaps about giving ecstatic little barks and squeals,
When ashamed, he drops his tail between his legs

questions.prompt: What does a dog seem to say when it stands at attention?
facilitatorNotes: “Well, what’s doing?” Comstock gives the dog a voice to show its alert, curious look, with one ear lifted.
evidence: looks up with one ear lifted as if to say, “Well, what’s doing?”

questions.prompt: Why would barking while chasing an animal seem foolish? How does Comstock explain it?
facilitatorNotes: It tells the hunted animal where the dog is. But dogs come from wolves that hunt in packs, and the barking keeps the pack together.
evidence: which would seem at first sight to be a foolish thing to do,
But it must be borne in mind that dogs are descended from wolves,

questions.prompt: Why does a dog howl at music, according to Comstock? What does she suggest music does to people?
facilitatorNotes: Music wakes the old wild habit of howling to call the pack. She suggests music also stirs strong, old feelings in people and frees us for a while from everyday rules. Readers can say whether music does that for them.
evidence: it is simply a reversion to the wild habit of howling to call together the pack
But perhaps that, too, is why we respond to music,

readings.title: The Cat — Jenny, who adopted a baby (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a true story from the writer’s own childhood, and trace how an animal learned a trick step by step.
readings.focus: A mother cat’s care for a human baby, and the same cat’s cleverness with door latches.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Here she tells about a cat from her own childhood. “As Rachel crying for her children” comes from the Bible and means mourning lost children. A latch is a door catch lifted by pressing a thumb-piece; futile means useless.
readings.contentNote: A wild cat kills Jenny’s kittens, and Jenny brings half-killed mice to the baby’s cradle.

excerpt.locator: “The Cat,” Teacher’s Story, first two paragraphs; opens “OF all people, the writer should regard the cat sympathetically, for when she was a baby…”; closes “…the rooms in this clever manner, and taught a few of her bright kittens to do the same.”.

questions.prompt: How did Jenny come to “adopt” the baby? What had just happened to her?
facilitatorNotes: She had lost her first kittens to a savage cat from the woods, and seemed to understand that the baby, though bigger than she was, was an infant.
evidence: lost her first litter of kittens,
she seemed suddenly to comprehend that I, although larger than she, was an infant.

questions.prompt: What did Jenny bring to the cradle? Why did it please the baby more than her mother?
facilitatorNotes: Half-killed mice to play with, as a mother cat brings prey to kittens. The baby liked it; her mother certainly did not. Comstock is joking about it now.
evidence: she brought half-killed mice and placed them enticingly in my cradle,
a performance which pleased me much more than it did my real mother.

questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, how Jenny learned to open latched doors.
facilitatorNotes: She played with the latch until people opened the door for her; one day she pushed it down by chance and the door opened; after that she always did it, then tried other doors, hanging by one front leg through the handle and pressing the thumb-piece with the other foot.
evidence: one day she chanced to push down the latch,
by thrusting one front leg through the handle,

questions.prompt: Jenny also tried the latches from the other side, then “soon ceased this futile waste of energy.” What does that tell you about how she learned?
facilitatorNotes: She tried, saw it did not work, and stopped: she learned from results, not only from habit. Some readers may say she simply gave up; either way, she noticed the difference.
evidence: she soon ceased this futile waste of energy;
taught a few of her bright kittens to do the same.

readings.title: The Horse — the voice and the hand (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument for kindness that rests on what a horse is like.
readings.focus: A good horseman trains by voice and care, not by the whip.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. In her time horses pulled carts, carriages and ploughs, and nearly every family depended on one. To epitomize is to sum up; to shy is to jump aside in fright. Timothy is a kind of hay grass. A bit is the metal bar in a horse’s mouth; a check-rein holds a horse’s head up, and pulled tight it hurts. Perspiration is sweat.
readings.contentNote: The passage mentions whipping and a cruel harness strap in order to argue against them.

excerpt.locator: “The Horse,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on training and on feeding and care; opens “An excellent horseman once said to me, “The whip may teach a horse to obey the voice, but…”; closes “…more attention during this process than its body, a fact not always well understood.”.

questions.prompt: What did the excellent horseman say about the whip and the voice?
facilitatorNotes: The whip may teach a horse to obey the voice, but a well-trained horse is controlled by voice and hand. He relied on the horse’s feelings.
evidence: “The whip may teach a horse to obey the voice, but the voice and hand control the well-broken horse,”
It is the horse’s feelings that I rely on.

questions.prompt: Why does a horse shy? Why does Comstock say the habit was once useful?
facilitatorNotes: Wild horses jumped aside to escape an enemy crouching in the grass. A habit that annoys us now once saved horses’ lives, so the voice, not a blow, should calm it.
evidence: the habit of shying was the wild horse’s method of escaping the crouching foe in the grass.

questions.prompt: Comstock gives a test for anyone who doubts that a frozen bit should be warmed. What is it, and why is it convincing?
facilitatorNotes: Put a frozen piece of steel in your own mouth. It makes the reader feel what the horse feels.
evidence: let him put a frozen piece of steel in his own mouth.

questions.prompt: Comstock says grooming is “a part of its rights.” What does she think people owe a horse? Do you agree that animals have rights?
facilitatorNotes: Regular food, warm water in winter, a warmed bit, a blanket when sweating in the cold, no tight check-rein, careful grooming. Calling these “rights” means they are owed, not favors. Readers may agree, or say kindness is a duty without calling it a right.
evidence: The grooming of a horse is a part of its rights,
The tight-drawn, cruel use of the over check-rein should not be permitted,

readings.title: The Pig — small eyes and a clever brain (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how a childhood memory leads into an argument.
readings.focus: Comstock argues that the pig, usually mocked, is the cleverest animal on the farm.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. To essay is to try; working buttonholes means sewing round them. “His pigship” is a joke title, like “his lordship.” Sagacity is wisdom; swine are pigs; in a story from the Christian Gospels, a herd of swine rushed into the sea. A poke is a sack: “buying a pig in a poke” means buying something without looking at it.

excerpt.locator: “The Pig,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on the pig’s eyes and intelligence; opens “When, as a small girl, I essayed the difficult task of working buttonholes, I was told if…”; closes “…when we say of other uncertain undertakings, that they are like “buying a pig in a poke.””.

questions.prompt: What made Comstock notice pigs’ eyes when she was a small girl?
facilitatorNotes: She was told her buttonholes would look like a pig’s eye if her stitches were too far apart. The remark made her observe pigs’ eyes ever after.
evidence: my buttonhole would look like a pig’s eye,
a remark which made me observant of that organ ever after.

questions.prompt: What evidence does Comstock give that the pig is intelligent?
facilitatorNotes: Its eyes “gleam with intelligence”; it has a good memory, learns tricks, follows its master like a dog; trained pigs pick out cards and count; wild hogs are full of strategy.
evidence: it has excellent memory and can be taught tricks readily;
Hunters of wild hogs proclaim that they are full of strategy and cunning,

questions.prompt: Why, according to Comstock, don’t farm pigs get a chance to use their brains? When do they show how clever they are?
facilitatorNotes: People stuff them with fattening food. They show their cleverness when they break out of the sty and refuse to be driven back.
evidence: we stuff it so with fattening food, that it does not have a chance to use its brain,
except now and then when it breaks out of the sty

questions.prompt: People often call someone a “pig” to insult them. After reading this, do you think pigs deserve their bad name? Use Comstock’s words.
facilitatorNotes: Comstock thinks they do not: “the most intelligent of all the farm animals, if it is only given a chance.” Readers may agree, or point out that she is one admirer. Ask what “if it is only given a chance” suggests about how we judge animals.
evidence: The pig is the most intelligent of all the farm animals, if it is only given a chance;

readings.title: The Monarch — caterpillar whips and a jewel of jade (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Picture two stages of one insect from close description, and notice when a scientist writes like a poet.
readings.focus: A striped caterpillar that waves its whips, and a chrysalis that looks like jewellery.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The monarch is an orange-and-black butterfly. Its caterpillar eats only milkweed; a chrysalis is the hard case in which the caterpillar changes into a butterfly. Succulent means juicy; segments are the rings of the body; filaments are threads. Ichneumon flies and other tiny parasitic flies lay eggs on caterpillars. Jade is a green stone; jet is a shiny black stone; garniture is decoration; palatable means good to eat.
readings.contentNote: Tiny fly grubs feed inside caterpillars and kill them.

excerpt.locator: “The Monarch Butterfly,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on the caterpillar and the chrysalis; opens “The milkweed caterpillar, which is the young of the monarch butterfly, is a striking…”; closes “…and darker hue. The butterfly emerges about twelve days after the change to a chrysalis.”.

questions.prompt: Describe the full-grown monarch caterpillar. What are its “whiplash-like organs” for?
facilitatorNotes: About two inches long, green with yellow and black stripes, with two long whips near the head and two at the rear. Comstock thinks they frighten away parasitic flies.
evidence: it is a gay creature, with ground color of green and cross stripes of yellow and black.
These filaments are undoubtedly of use in frightening away the little parasitic flies,

questions.prompt: What memory from childhood does Comstock share? Why does she add it?
facilitatorNotes: As a child she felt “creepy” watching the caterpillars lash their whips. If the flies were as frightened as she was, the caterpillars were safe. The memory makes the whips’ purpose easy to believe.
evidence: I remember well when I was a child, the creepy feeling
if the ichneumon flies were as frightened as I, the caterpillars were surely safe.

questions.prompt: How do the caterpillar’s colors protect it in two different ways?
facilitatorNotes: The bright colors warn birds it tastes bad; when it drops into the grass, the same stripes hide it from less fussy animals.
evidence: Its striking colors undoubtedly defend it from birds,
their stripes make them very inconspicuous among the grass

questions.prompt: Comstock calls the chrysalis “the most beautiful gem in Nature’s jewel casket.” Find the words that make it sound like jewellery. Is this good science writing, or too fancy?
facilitatorNotes: Jade, gold-foil, jet, gilt buttons, garniture. The words help readers picture exact colors; she even tests the gold with a lens. Some will find it lovely, others too much; both can point to “I maintain,” which marks it as her opinion.
evidence: The monarch chrysalis is, I maintain, the most beautiful gem in Nature’s jewel casket;
we cannot but believe that they are bits of polished gold-foil.

readings.title: The Firefly — the summer sowing of lights (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Work out what Comstock means by “sowing” and “harvest” when she writes about lights.
readings.focus: Fireflies flash on purpose, by their own will, to find their mates.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The Teacher’s Story opens with three lines by the poet James Whitcomb Riley. To sow is to scatter seeds; the harvest is what grows from them. Fireflies are beetles. Refulgent means shining brightly; curlicues are curly loops; ardor is eager energy; phosphorescent wood is rotting wood that glows faintly; edifying means teaching something worth learning; voluntarily means by choice.

excerpt.locator: “The Firefly,” Teacher’s Story, from the opening lines of verse through the second paragraph; opens “And lavishly to left and right, The fireflies, like golden seeds, Are sown upon the night.”; closes “…brilliant, for the flashing of their lights is for the attraction of their mates.”.

questions.prompt: When do fireflies make their lights, and when do they stop?
facilitatorNotes: On warm, damp nights in July and August, and some in September, from early twilight until the night grows cold.
evidence: during warm, damp nights in July and August,
lasts until the cold atmosphere of the later night dampens the firefly ardor!

questions.prompt: How do different kinds of fireflies flash differently?
facilitatorNotes: Some fly near the grass, others above our heads; some blink briefly, some give longer flashes that show their direction, and one southern kind draws “gleaming curlicues.”
evidence: some species hover next to the grass, others fly above our heads,
which gives such long flashes that they mark the night with gleaming curlicues.

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock find the firefly’s flash “startling” to people?
facilitatorNotes: The flash is clearly done on purpose, by the beetle’s will, while people “cannot even blush or turn pale voluntarily.” The insect can do something we cannot.
evidence: it is so evidently an act of will on the part of the beetle,
who cannot even blush or turn pale voluntarily.

questions.prompt: Riley says the fireflies are “like golden seeds” sown upon the night, and Comstock carries the picture on. What might the “harvest” be? And what two meanings does she play with in “socially brilliant”?
facilitatorNotes: Brilliant means both shining and very good company; the flashing is “for the attraction of their mates,” so the harvest may be the mates the lights bring together, which few people ever notice. Readers may suggest other harvests, such as the next summer’s fireflies.
evidence: The fireflies, like golden seeds,
How little most of us know of the harvest,
for the flashing of their lights is for the attraction of their mates.

readings.title: The Ant-Nest — the ant nurses (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow the life stages of an ant and the jobs the nurses do at each one.
readings.focus: Worker ants care for their young sisters with surprising gentleness, and sometimes impatience.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Comstock kept ants in glass-sided nests so she could watch them. An ant hatches from an egg as a larva (plural larvæ), a soft grub; then it becomes a pupa (plural pupæ) before it is a grown ant. The workers are all sisters. Regurgitated food is food brought back up from the stomach; the alimentary canal is the food tube through the body; draughts are drafts of cool air. Miss Fielde was Adele Fielde, who studied ants. A “callow” is a newly hatched grown ant.

excerpt.locator: “The Ant-Nest, and What May Be Seen Within It,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on the nurses and the young; opens “The ants seem to realize the cost and care of rearing their young; and when a nest is…”; closes “…by the waist, and carry her off with an air that says plainly, “Come along, you stupid!””.

questions.prompt: When a nest is attacked, which young are saved first? Why might that be?
facilitatorNotes: The oldest, usually the pupæ. Comstock thinks the ants “realize the cost and care of rearing their young”: the oldest have had the most care and are nearest to being grown.
evidence: the oldest, which are usually in the pupa stage, are saved first.

questions.prompt: What did Comstock see when she gave her ants some hard-boiled egg yolk?
facilitatorNotes: The nurses dumped the larvæ around its edges to eat, and she could see the yellow yolk through their see-through bodies, all the way along.
evidence: the ant nurses dumped the larvæ down around the edges of it;
I could see the yellow of the egg the whole length of the alimentary canal.

questions.prompt: How do the nurses carry the pupæ? Why does Comstock say people are wrong to call pupæ “ants’ eggs”?
facilitatorNotes: Gently, by the loose pupal skin, “like carrying a baby by its clothes.” Pupæ are almost as large as an ant; real ants’ eggs are no bigger than pin points.
evidence: she holds them by the loose pupal skin, like carrying a baby by its clothes.
Ants’ eggs are not larger than pin points.

questions.prompt: Comstock makes the ants sound like people: a “graded school,” “baby sisters,” “Come along, you stupid!” Find one more example. Does this help you understand the ants, or does it make them seem too human?
facilitatorNotes: Other examples: a callow curls up “like a kitten,” the nurses “make a toilet,” the callows are “herded together.” The comparisons make the behavior easy to picture; but ants do not speak, and “Come along, you stupid!” is her joke. Readers should tell what she saw from what she imagined.
evidence: carry her off with an air that says plainly, “Come along, you stupid!”
if she takes her by the waist the callow curls up like a kitten,

readings.title: The Yellow-Jacket — a polite guest at the camp table (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Test a surprising claim against the evidence of years of watching.
readings.focus: Wasps that share a family’s meals do no harm to people who stay calm.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Yellow-jackets are black-and-yellow wasps. “Waspish” means bad-tempered. Viands are foods; to palpitate is to beat or throb; a finger bowl is a small bowl of water for rinsing the fingers at a fancy dinner.
readings.contentNote: Yellow-jackets can sting; a reader who is allergic to stings should not test Comstock’s advice.

excerpt.locator: “The Yellow-Jacket,” Teacher’s Story, the first paragraph; opens “MANY wasps are not so waspish after all when we understand one important fact about them;…”; closes “…front feet by passing them through her jaws, which is a wasp way of using a finger bowl.”.

questions.prompt: What “important fact” about wasps does Comstock say people need to understand?
facilitatorNotes: Wasps are very nervous themselves and “detest that quality in others”: they dislike nervousness in the creatures around them.
evidence: although they are very nervous themselves, they detest that quality in others.

questions.prompt: What do the yellow-jackets do at the family’s camp meals?
facilitatorNotes: They inspect the food, fan the family’s faces with their wings, choose sweet fruit, and even swoop on the roast beef like a hawk.
evidence: They make inquisitive tours of inspection over the viands on the table,
seizing a tidbit as a hawk does a chicken.

questions.prompt: Why does the family stay calm? What is the only way they expect to be stung?
facilitatorNotes: They know that unless they accidentally pinch a wasp, they will not be harmed. Calm people do not alarm the nervous wasps.
evidence: We always remain calm during these visitations,
unless we inadvertently pinch one, we shall not be harmed;

questions.prompt: Comstock says the wasps are “extra polite in their manners.” What evidence does she give? Is “polite” a fair word for a wasp?
facilitatorNotes: After eating syrup, a wasp cleans its front feet by passing them through its jaws: “a wasp way of using a finger bowl.” Some readers will enjoy the joke; others may say the wasp is just cleaning, not being polite. Both can be right about different things.
evidence: They are extra polite in their manners,
which is a wasp way of using a finger bowl.

readings.title: The Leaf-cutter Bee — a basket made of rose leaves (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Tell what the writer actually saw from what she explains from earlier knowledge.
readings.focus: A small bee cuts rose leaves and builds a row of sealed cradles for her young.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Pollen is the yellow dust of flowers; nectar is their sweet juice; a cavity is a hollow space; saliva is spit. Honey-bees carry pollen in “baskets” on their legs. The book’s “base drum” is a bass drum.

excerpt.locator: “The Leaf-cutter Bee,” Teacher’s Story, first two paragraphs; opens “ONE beautiful day in late June when I was picking some roses, I saw a bee, almost as…”; closes “…perhaps makes ten or more, placing one cup just ahead of another in the little tunnel.”.

questions.prompt: What did Comstock see the bee do on the rose bush? What comparison does she use for the bee flying off with its load?
facilitatorNotes: It cut a circle out of a leaf with its jaws in a wink and flew off holding it, the green disk as big for the bee as a bass drum hung on a small drummer.
evidence: cut a circle out of a leaf with her jaws
as large in proportion to her size as a big base drum hung to the neck of a small drummer.

questions.prompt: The second paragraph begins “I knew the story of the little bee.” Which part did Comstock see with her own eyes, and which part does she tell from what she already knew?
facilitatorNotes: She saw only the cutting, and then found the holes in the leaves; the bee never came back. The tunnel, cups, pollen, egg and lids come from her knowledge, which is why she writes “perhaps,” “maybe” and “probably.”
evidence: I waited long for her to come back, but she came not;
perhaps she had tunneled it herself

questions.prompt: Put the bee’s work in order, from the tunnel to the lid.
facilitatorNotes: She finds or digs a tunnel; folds long leaf pieces into a thimble-shaped cup glued with saliva; fills it with a paste of pollen and nectar; lays an egg; cuts round lids to seal it; then builds more cups in a row.
evidence: made it into a pasty mass and heaped it at the bottom of the cup;
and then she laid an egg upon it;

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock call the bee “a nice mathematician”?
facilitatorNotes: Nice here means exact. She cuts each lid just a little larger than the cup’s rim so it can be pushed in and fit tightly.
evidence: She is a nice mathematician and she cuts the lid just a little larger than the rim of the cup,

readings.title: The Garden Snail — eyes on stalks (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Picture a comparison exactly, and test whether the writer’s evidence supports her conclusion.
readings.focus: A snail that folds up and unfolds, sees with stalked eyes, and seems to know where it wants to go.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. A tramp is a wanderer who carries everything with him; a hermitage is a hermit’s lonely home; topography is the shape of the land; a piazza is a porch.

excerpt.locator: “The Garden Snail,” Teacher’s Story, second paragraph; opens “Never was an animal so capable of stretching out and then folding up all its organs, as…”; closes “…was determined to go crosswise and crawl under the edge, where it was nice and dark.”.

questions.prompt: What happens when you turn a snail on its back and wait?
facilitatorNotes: After a while the folded tail end of the foot pushes out, and then the head and horns come “bubbling out.”
evidence: the hind end of the foot, which was folded together, pushes forth;
then the head and horns come bubbling out.

questions.prompt: What are a snail’s long “horns” really? Explain the marble-and-glove comparison.
facilitatorNotes: Stalks with an eye at each tip. To pull an eye back, the snail draws it down inside the stalk, the way a marble on a glove fingertip could be pulled back through the middle of the finger.
evidence: each is a stalk bearing an eye on the tip.
like a marble fastened to the tip of a glove finger.

questions.prompt: What are the shorter horns for?
facilitatorNotes: They are feelers, used all the time to test the surface the snail is crawling on.
evidence: they are used constantly for testing the nature of the surface on which the snail is crawling.

questions.prompt: Comstock is “convinced that snails have decided views about where they wish to go.” What evidence does she give? Does it convince you?
facilitatorNotes: She tried for hours to keep snails crawling along the porch railing, and every one turned crosswise to crawl under the edge “where it was nice and dark.” Some readers will agree; others will say the snails were seeking dark, damp places rather than having opinions.
evidence: I have tried by the hour to keep them marching lengthwise on the piazza railing,
every snail was determined to go crosswise and crawl under the edge, where it was nice and dark.

readings.title: The Earthworm — the little plowman (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Match each part of the earthworm’s work with the farmer’s job it is compared to.
readings.focus: A small, overlooked animal does every job a farmer does to the soil.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. To till is to work the soil for growing crops. A harrow is a farm tool dragged over plowed ground to break up lumps; a gizzard is a muscular stomach that grinds food with sand or grit. Amendments are things added to improve soil, such as lime; fertilizers feed plants; drainage carries away extra water. An agriculturist is a farmer.

excerpt.locator: “The Earthworm,” Teacher’s Story, the first two paragraphs; opens “The earthworm is, among lower animals, essentially the farmer. Long before man conceived…”; closes “…plants by cultivating, that is keeping fine and granular, the soil about the roots.”.

questions.prompt: What does Comstock call the earthworm in the first sentence? Why does she say it was there first?
facilitatorNotes: “Essentially the farmer.” It was plowing, harrowing and fertilizing the land “long before man conceived the idea of tilling the soil.”
evidence: The earthworm is, among lower animals, essentially the farmer.
Long before man conceived the idea of tilling the soil,

questions.prompt: How does the earthworm “plow” and “harrow”?
facilitatorNotes: It plows by bringing subsoil up from deep down; it harrows by grinding soil in its sand-filled gizzard, making it finer than a rake can.
evidence: bringing to the surface the subsoil, which is exactly what we do when we plow deeply.
the earthworm grinds it in a gizzard stocked with grains of sand or fine gravel,

questions.prompt: Name two more farm jobs the earthworm does, and how.

evidence: They plant seeds by covering those that lie on the ground with soil from below the surface
but they bore holes to some depth which carry off the surplus water.

questions.prompt: Comstock uses one comparison, the worm as farmer, all the way through. Why is that a good way to teach about earthworms? Does the comparison go too far anywhere?
facilitatorNotes: Readers already know what a farmer does, so each job makes the worm’s work clear and important. But worms do not plan: “have never studied any system of drainage” admits it. Some may think “adept in the use of fertilizers” goes too far.
evidence: These minute agriculturists have never studied any system of drainage,
The earthworm is apparently an adept in the use of fertilizers;

questions.prompt: How does the crayfish start digging her nest?
facilitatorNotes: At one side of the tank she pushes her feelers and nippers down between the glass and the stones, grabs a pebble in each claw and pulls it up.
evidence: she seizes a pebble in each claw and pulls it up

questions.prompt: Comstock compares the crayfish to a lady and to a schoolboy. What is each comparison describing?
facilitatorNotes: Tucking her tail under her body is like a lady tucking up her skirts for work; holding the load down with her jaw-feet is like a schoolboy steadying a pile of books with his chin.
evidence: as a lady tucks up her skirts
just as I have seen a schoolboy use his chin,

questions.prompt: What does one crayfish do with the earthworm she is given? Which words describe what happened, and which describe what Comstock thinks the crayfish felt?

evidence: spitefully threw down both worm and pebble on top of her fellow prisoner,
the most eloquent of crayfish profanity.

questions.prompt: What did Comstock see when a daddy-longlegs walked into a drop of water?
facilitatorNotes: Its foot never got wet, because it touched the water’s surface so lightly.
evidence: I have seen a “daddy” walk into a drop of water and his foot was never wetted,

questions.prompt: Which legs are longest, and what are they used for?
facilitatorNotes: The second pair. They explore the surroundings; when he runs, he spreads them wide and keeps them moving, feeling things by touch.
evidence: The legs of the second pair are ordinarily used in exploring the surroundings.
these two legs are spread wide apart and keep in rapid motion;

questions.prompt: How long would your legs be if they were as long, for your size, as a daddy-longlegs’ legs? Why does Comstock give this comparison?

evidence: If our legs were as long in comparison as his, they would be about forty feet in length.

questions.prompt: When the long legs sense food, the daddy-longlegs changes how it moves. Describe it. Why does it move this way?
facilitatorNotes: It teeters, tipping its body down at every step, so its palpi can explore the ground below; it can stretch them out to test a substance. Readers may compare it with how they would check a strange food.
evidence: he commences a peculiar teetering motion of the body,
they can be extended out quite a distance if “daddy” wishes to test a substance.

readings.title: The Evening Primrose — a flower that opens at dusk (excerpt)

readings.focus: The sudden opening of a flower at evening, watched closely and timed.

evidence: Then some warm evening, usually about sunset,
the long tube which looks like the flower stem has been turning yellow;

questions.prompt: How does the umbrella comparison help explain why one petal seems to do all the work?
facilitatorNotes: The petals are wrapped round each other like a folded umbrella, so one petal’s edge comes free first and seems to lead, though all of them are pushing.
evidence: they are wrapped around each other in the bud as an umbrella is folded,

questions.prompt: How long does the opening take? What reasons does Comstock give for the difference?
facilitatorNotes: Once half an hour, another time two or three minutes. She suggests it depends on the flower’s vigor, and says garden kinds open faster than wild ones.
evidence: once I watched for half an hour to see it accomplished, and again I have seen it done in two or three minutes.

questions.prompt: Comstock says it is hard “not to attribute to them consciousness of action.” What does she mean? Find another place where she writes as if the flower could want something.
facilitatorNotes: It is hard not to feel the petals mean to open, because they move so fast. She also says the petals are “pushing for freedom” and that the sepals “seem to try to repress them.” She knows it is a plant; the speed tempts her, and us.
evidence: all the others are pushing for freedom;
which seem to try to repress them.

readings.title: The Milkweed — a pod like a hammock full of babies (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a description step by step as if opening the pod yourself.
readings.focus: The milkweed pod is a carefully made house for seeds and silk.

excerpt.locator: “The Milkweed,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraph on the pod; opens “The milkweed pod has been the admiration of nature students from the beginning, and…”; closes “…of babies, except that the milkweed babies are fastened on the outside of the hammock.”.

questions.prompt: What does Comstock admire first about a green milkweed pod?
facilitatorNotes: Its beautiful shape, and the rows of raised points along the seam, “like embossed embroidery” on its soft, felty surface.
evidence: we first admire its beautiful shape;
suggests embossed embroidery.

questions.prompt: What did Comstock do with milkweed pods when she was a child?
facilitatorNotes: She and other children emptied the pods and shut bumblebees inside “to hear them sing,” but always let them go. Now she thinks the pod’s own contents are more interesting.
evidence: we imprisoned therein bumblebees “to hear them sing,” but we always let them go again.

questions.prompt: What three things are inside the pod?
facilitatorNotes: A line of white velvet (the seed-support), brown seeds overlapping with their “heads all in one direction,” and shining milkweed silk.
evidence: Below the opening is a line of white velvet;
the exquisite milkweed silk

questions.prompt: Comstock compares the pod’s seam to finished cloth, its silk to a skein, and the seed-support to “a hammock full of babies.” Which comparison helps you see the pod best? Why does she use words from sewing?
facilitatorNotes: Any choice with a reason works. Sewing words (selvage, embroidery, skein, reel) fit because the pod looks carefully made, as if by a skilled hand; she says no human reel could give such shine. The hammock image makes the seeds seem cared for.
evidence: It is like a hammock full of babies,
no human reel could give us a skein of such luster.

readings.title: The Mullein — a plant the sheep will not eat (excerpt)

readings.focus: A writer tastes a weed to find out how it survives, and discovers its real enemy.

excerpt.locator: “Mullein,” Teacher’s Story, second paragraph; opens “I was wandering one day in a sheep pasture and looking curiously at the few plants left…”; closes “…of a snout beetle, which is a far more dangerous enemy of the mullein than is the sheep.”.

questions.prompt: What question did Comstock ask the mullein, and how did she try to answer it?
facilitatorNotes: Why don’t the sheep like you; are you bitter? She took a bite herself. It did not taste bitter, but her tongue burned from the prickly felt on the leaf.
evidence: Why do the sheep not relish you? Are you bitter?
my tongue smarted and burned for some time after,

questions.prompt: What trick did her grandmother once play on her, and what did she learn from it?
facilitatorNotes: She was told that rubbing her cheeks with mullein would make her beautiful; her cheeks turned red and then purple. She learned that comfort matters more than beauty, and later, under a microscope, why: the felt is made of sharp little spikes.
evidence: she told me that to be beautiful, I needed only to rub my cheeks with mullein leaves,
No wonder my cheeks were red one day and purple the next,

questions.prompt: Find two ways the mullein protects itself. What does each one protect it from?
facilitatorNotes: The felt keeps grazing animals away and stops the leaves drying out in drought; the deep taproot reaches water and food below other plants.
evidence: keeps the mullein safe from grazing animals
reached below most other plants for moisture and food.

questions.prompt: The mullein beats the sheep, but Comstock finds a “far more dangerous enemy.” What is it? Why is it more dangerous?
facilitatorNotes: Little white grubs, young snout beetles, living inside the seed capsules. Sheep only fail to eat the leaves, but the grubs eat the seeds, the plant’s future plants.
evidence: They were the young of a snout beetle, which is a far more dangerous enemy of the mullein than is the sheep.

readings.title: The Pumpkin — two kinds of flowers and their treasure (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Keep two kinds of flower apart and work out why the pumpkin needs both, and the bee.
readings.focus: A pumpkin grows only when bees carry pollen from one kind of blossom to the other.

Liliputian means tiny, from the little people of Lilliput in Gulliver’s Travels. Corrugations are ridges; secretes means gives off.

excerpt.locator: “The Pumpkin,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on the two kinds of blossom; opens “The story of the treasure at the heart of this starry, bell-shaped flower is a double…”; closes “…it to the one which needs it, as this is the only way that the fruit may be developed.”.

questions.prompt: How can you tell which pumpkin flower will become a pumpkin?
facilitatorNotes: It has a little green globe, the ovary, below it.
evidence: selecting a flower that has below it a little green globe—the ovary—which will later develop into a pumpkin.

questions.prompt: What do the stigmas look like, and what must a bee do to reach the nectar in that flower?
facilitatorNotes: Like tiny boxing-gloves on posts. The bee must “stand on her head” and brush her pollen-dusty side against them.
evidence: three stigmas, that look like liliputian boxing-gloves;
the lady bee must stand on her head

questions.prompt: Some people said bees visit the other kind of flower only for pollen. What did Comstock find?
facilitatorNotes: Three small openings at the base of the pedestal; bees push their tongues through them, and below is a velvet-lined “treasure cave” with nectar she could taste. “I am convinced that this is not all of the story.”
evidence: I am convinced that this is not all of the story.
we shall find below the latter, a treasure cave;

questions.prompt: Why does the pumpkin need bees? What would happen without them?
facilitatorNotes: Only insects carry pollen from the flower that makes it to the flower that needs it; without them no pumpkins would grow. Ask what else in a garden depends on bees.
evidence: The pumpkin is absolutely dependent upon the work of bees and other insects
as this is the only way that the fruit may be developed.

readings.title: The Brook — a gang of workmen (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a long comparison and use it to explain what a muddy stream is doing.
readings.focus: A brook is busiest when it is muddy: every drop digs and carries.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York.
