Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. Limpid means clear; roily means muddy and stirred up. Gravity is the pull that makes water flow downhill. Sediment is the sand and mud that water lets fall.

excerpt.locator: “The Brook,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraph on the brook as digger and carrier; opens “But the brook is not simply an object to look at and admire; it is a very busy worker,…”; closes “…always dropped first, and that the fine mud is carried farthest before it is deposited.”.

questions.prompt: When is the brook doing the least work, and when is it working hardest?
facilitatorNotes: Least when its water is perfectly clear; hardest when it is “roily,” usually after rain.
evidence: when its waters are perfectly clear—the stream is doing the least work.
when the waters are roily the brook is working very hard.

questions.prompt: Poets talk about the brook “playing.” What does Comstock say it is really doing?
facilitatorNotes: Digging and carrying: each drop snatches up a little earth and uses it to knock loose more. The muddy water shows the load.
evidence: it is a very busy worker, its chief labor being that of a digger and carrier.
snatches up a tiny load of earth and carries it along.

questions.prompt: What happens when the brook reaches level ground? In what order does it drop its load?
facilitatorNotes: The drops “act tired” and let their loads fall: gravel and rocks first, fine soil last and farthest.
evidence: the drops act tired and seem to have no ambition to pick up more soil,
the gravel is always dropped first, and that the fine mud is carried farthest

questions.prompt: Comstock calls the brook “a gang of workmen each of which is using its own load as a tool.” How does this picture help explain why a flood digs so much? Can you think of another picture for it?
facilitatorNotes: More water means more drops, each with a crowbar or pickaxe, working together and fast; so the channel grows deeper and wider. Readers might suggest an army, a crowd of shovellers, or a conveyor belt; ask which fits best.
evidence: On and on the brook flows, a gang of workmen each of which is using its own load as a tool,
uses its own little load of earth or gravel as a crowbar or pickaxe

readings.title: The Magnet — a mystery we can play with (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Separate what we know a magnet does from what we do not know it is.
readings.focus: The magnet was once thought magic, and still holds a mystery, but children can test its powers.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The Arabian Nights is an old collection of tales. Lodestone is a natural magnetic rock; mariners are sailors; medieval navigation means finding the way at sea in the Middle Ages. To repel is to push away; poles are the two ends of a magnet; cohesion is sticking together. Professor George L. Burr was a Cornell historian.

excerpt.locator: “The Magnet,” Teacher’s Story, the first paragraph; opens “UNTIL comparatively recent times, the power of the magnet was so inexplicable that it was…”; closes “…be demonstrated by a competition between magnets, noting how many tacks each will hold.”.

questions.prompt: What did sailors of the Middle Ages believe about a magnetic island?
facilitatorNotes: That a mountain island of lodestone pulled the nails out of passing ships and wrecked them. The fear even shaped how they sailed.
evidence: the island that pulled the nails from passing ships and thus wrecked them
this mountain of lodestone and the fear which it inspired

questions.prompt: Comstock says, “We know what it does, but we do not know what it is.” Name two things she says we know a magnet does.
facilitatorNotes: Force flows from the ends; unlike ends attract and like ends repel; there is less force halfway between the poles; the force reaches across a gap; it can pass to iron tacks to make a chain.
evidence: We know what it does, but we do not know what it is.
there is less of this force at a point in the magnet half-way between the poles;

questions.prompt: What does the chain of tacks show? What happens when the tacks are taken off the magnet?
facilitatorNotes: The magnet can pass its force to iron objects, so each tack holds the next. Taken off, they no longer stick together.
evidence: the child takes up a chain of tacks at the end of the magnet;
the tacks when removed from the magnet have no such power of cohesion.

questions.prompt: Describe the game of “stealing tacks.” Why is a game a good way to learn about magnets?
facilitatorNotes: A stronger magnet takes tacks away from a weaker one, which shows that some magnets are stronger. Playing lets children test and compare for themselves instead of only being told. Ask what else could be tested with two magnets.
evidence: the favorite game of “stealing tacks,” the stronger magnet taking them away from the weaker;

readings.title: The Story of the Stars — suns, double stars and light-years (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Hold onto very large numbers by using Comstock’s comparisons, and notice where science has learned more since.
readings.focus: Every star is a sun, many are pairs, and their light has travelled for years to reach us.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. A telescope makes faraway things look nearer; a spectroscope splits starlight into colors and shows what a star is made of. An orbit is the path one body travels around another. The Pole-star is the North Star; the Pleiades are a small cluster of stars.

excerpt.locator: “The Story of the Stars,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on what the stars are and how far away they are; opens “Thus, we have learned many things about the stars; we know that every shining star is a…”; closes “…was discovered. Most of the stars are so far away that we cannot measure the distance.”.

questions.prompt: What does Comstock say every shining star really is? What did she think some stars might have?
facilitatorNotes: A great blazing sun. She thought many might have worlds like the earth spinning round them, too far away to see. Since the 1990s astronomers have found thousands of such planets.
evidence: we know that every shining star is a great blazing sun,
there is no reason to doubt that many of these suns have worlds, like the earth, spinning around them

questions.prompt: What is a double star? How long do different pairs take to circle each other?
facilitatorNotes: Two suns that swing round a common center but look like one star. Some take five years, others sixteen or forty-six, one “lazy pair” about sixteen hundred, and some only a few hours.
evidence: made up of two vast suns swinging around a common center;
there is at least one lazy pair which seems to require fully sixteen hundred years

questions.prompt: What is a light-year, and why do astronomers use it?
facilitatorNotes: The distance light travels in a year, about six trillion miles. Distances in miles are too large to grasp.
evidence: this distance is called a light-year.
when this distance is expressed in miles it is too much for us to grasp.

questions.prompt: Comstock says the light from the Pole-star left it “almost half a century ago.” Astronomers now measure it as over four hundred years. What does that tell you about reading an old science book? Why is it still worth reading?
facilitatorNotes: Measurements improve, so numbers in old books may be out of date; check them against newer sources. But her main idea is still right: starlight is old light, and looking at a star is looking into the past. Readers may find that idea the most amazing part.
evidence: the light which reaches our eyes left that star almost half a century ago,
the light we get from the Pleiades may have started on its journey before America was discovered.

readings.title: The Pole-star and the Dippers — finding the North Star (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow directions that you can test on the next clear night.
readings.focus: The Big Dipper’s pointers lead to the North Star, which stays in our sky all night.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The Big Dipper is a group of seven bright stars shaped like a long-handled cup. The earth’s axis is the imaginary line it spins around, through the North and South Poles. The Northern Hemisphere is the half of the earth north of the equator. A mariner’s compass is a sailor’s compass; a coincidence is two things that happen together by chance.

excerpt.locator: “The Pole-star and the Dippers,” Teacher’s Story, the first paragraph; opens “The way to begin star study is to learn to know the Big Dipper, and through its pointers…”; closes “…to be nearly in the direction toward which the northern end of the compass needle points.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock say star study should begin with the Big Dipper and the Pole-star?
facilitatorNotes: They give a fixed starting point for finding any other star.
evidence: so as to have some fixed point to start from.

questions.prompt: How do you find the Pole-star from the Big Dipper? Try drawing it.
facilitatorNotes: Draw a line through the two outer stars of the bowl and continue it: it reaches the Pole-star. These two are called the pointers.
evidence: A line drawn through the outer two stars of the bowl, if extended, will touch the North Star, or Pole-star.

questions.prompt: Why does the Pole-star never set for people in the Northern Hemisphere? Is there a South Pole-star?
facilitatorNotes: The northern end of the earth’s axis points almost straight at it, so it stays above the North Pole while the sky seems to turn. There is no convenient South Pole-star.
evidence: the northern end of the earth’s axis is directed toward it,
so there is no South Pole-star.

questions.prompt: Comstock says twice that something is only a coincidence. What are the two coincidences? Why does she bother to point them out?
facilitatorNotes: That the Pole-star lies where the earth’s axis points, and that a compass needle points nearly toward it. She wants readers not to think the star pulls on the earth or the compass; her blackboard-and-pointer comparison makes the same point. Ask why it matters not to mix up “happens together” with “causes.”
evidence: the North Star has nothing to do with the axis of our earth any more than the figure on the blackboard has to do with the pointer;
It is also a coincidence that the needle of the mariner’s compass points toward the North Star;
